title: Saving a CPG client $2.4M on trade promotions
text:
The problem
A CPG client (a major US retailer) planned trade promotions off out-of-stock forecasts that were too coarse to trust at the SKU × store level, so promo spend and safety stock were routinely mis-sized. The business needed accurate, per-series demand forecasts across a very large portfolio — 300,000+ SKU × store series over a 2TB dataset — refreshed with automated backtesting and hyperparameter tuning, fast enough to plan against.

title: Saving a CPG client $2.4M on trade promotions
text:
The finding


Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
t = np.arange(60)
base = 100 + 18 * np.sin(t / 6)
actual = base + rng.normal(0, 5, 60)
actual[20:24] += 40          # a promotion spike
fc = base.copy(); fc[20:24] += 34

BG, FG, MUTED, GRID = "#0e1016", "#f4f5f7", "#9aa3b2", "#22262f"
A1, A2 = "#6366f1", "#22d3ee"

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.2))
fig.patch.set_facecolor(BG); ax.set_facecolor(BG)
ax.fill_between(t, fc - 10, fc + 10, color=A2, alpha=0.15, label="80% interval")
ax.plot(t, actual, color=MUTED, lw=1.6, label="actual")
ax.plot(t, fc, color=A1, lw=2.6, label="forecast")
ax.axvspan(20, 23, color="#fbbf24", alpha=0.25, label="promotion")
ax.set_xlabel("week", color=MUTED); ax.set_ylabel("units", color=MUTED)
ax.tick_params(colors=MUTED)
leg = ax.legend(frameon=False, ncol=2, labelcolor=FG)
for s in ["top", "right"]: ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["left"].set_color(GRID); ax.spines["bottom"].set_color(GRID)
ax.grid(axis="y", color=GRID, lw=1)
plt.tight_layout()
fig.savefig("hero.png", dpi=120, bbox_inches="tight", facecolor=BG)
plt.show()








Figure 1: Per-series forecast vs. actuals with prediction interval. Replace the synthetic series with a representative real backtest window.





Getting the promotion weeks right (the yellow band) is where the savings came from — that’s where a generic forecast fails and money is left on the table.

title: Saving a CPG client $2.4M on trade promotions
text:
Decisions and tradeoffs
Training a separate model per series (300k+ of them, over a 2TB dataset) was a deliberate choice over one global model: it captured per-SKU, per-store seasonality and promo response that a pooled model washed out, at the cost of a much heavier training and orchestration burden. I ran this on a distributed stack (PySpark / Databricks / Dask) with automated backtesting and hyperparameter tuning per series, so the whole portfolio could retrain on 100M+ rows a day. [[TODO: confirm exact model family — gradient boosting? statistical (ETS/ARIMA)? A related engagement (Russia, 50k models) reached 84% accuracy on high-quality segments, then added a Temporal Fusion Transformer for cross-learning across series for a further 17% uplift — worth confirming whether the same TFT cross-learning step applied here, since it’s a strong, specific technical detail if so.]]
The failure mode was under-forecasting: a coarser, less granular forecast doesn’t just miss on average — it systematically under-calls demand in the exact promotion weeks that matter most for stocking decisions, which is what drove the $2.4M in avoided stockout and expiry losses once the per-series approach replaced it. The tradeoff was real: per-series models are expensive to retrain at this scale, which is why the distributed backtesting/tuning pipeline mattered as much as the modeling choice itself.

title: Saving a CPG client $2.4M on trade promotions
text:
Measurement and limitations
Impact was measured as ~$2.4M in avoided stockout and expiry losses for the client, confirmed against the incumbent (coarser) forecasting process [[TODO: exact measurement window and the accuracy metric used — MAPE/WAPE — for the interview-ready version of this number]]. Honest limitations: cold-start SKUs with little promo history are the weakest segment (the Russia engagement’s 50k-model / 84%-accuracy split specifically called out this high-quality vs. low-quality segment gap), and the per-series design is expensive enough to retrain that refresh cadence is itself a cost tradeoff, not a free dial to turn.

title: Helping a CMO plan marketing spend with an LLM agent, not a dashboard
text:
Decisions and tradeoffs
I split the problem into retrieval (grounding answers in the right context) and answer synthesis over structured data, rather than asking one prompt to do everything — that made each half testable and each failure debuggable. On the retrieval side, I compared semantic vs. sparse search rather than defaulting to one, since marketing questions mix fuzzy (“campaigns similar to…”) and exact-match (“Q3 spend on…”) lookups that favor different retrieval methods. Worth noting for credibility: this took 2nd place in Tiger Analytics’ internal hackathon rather than shipping to a live CMO in production — an internal build-off result, not a production deployment claim.

title: Cutting alert fatigue 35% for an ops monitoring team
text:
The problem
This draws on two related builds: a multi-algorithm Anomaly Detection Accelerator with automated root-cause analysis over time-series data (Tiger Analytics), and a configurable, correlation-based fraud-detection platform for payroll data (Globant) — the closer match to “correlated, multivariate signals,” since payroll components naturally move together and a component that breaks that correlation is the actual fraud signal. On the payroll platform specifically, the existing approach flagged each payroll component against its own static threshold, which fired constantly on normal correlated movement and cost analyst time chasing false alarms while eroding trust in the system. The goal was to keep recall on genuine fraud while sharply cutting that false-positive rate.

title: Cutting alert fatigue 35% for an ops monitoring team
text:
The finding


Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
t = np.arange(200)
sig = np.sin(t / 9) + 0.4 * np.sin(t / 3) + rng.normal(0, 0.15, 200)
anom = np.array([40, 96, 150, 178])
sig[anom] += np.array([1.8, -1.6, 2.0, -1.7])

BG, FG, MUTED, GRID = "#0e1016", "#f4f5f7", "#9aa3b2", "#22262f"

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.2))
fig.patch.set_facecolor(BG); ax.set_facecolor(BG)
ax.plot(t, sig, color=MUTED, lw=1.3)
ax.scatter(anom, sig[anom], color="#f87171", s=42, zorder=3,
           edgecolors=BG, lw=0.8, label="detected anomaly")
ax.legend(frameon=False, labelcolor=FG)
ax.set_xlabel("time", color=MUTED); ax.set_ylabel("signal", color=MUTED)
ax.tick_params(colors=MUTED)
for s in ["top", "right"]: ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["left"].set_color(GRID); ax.spines["bottom"].set_color(GRID)
ax.grid(axis="y", color=GRID, lw=1)
plt.tight_layout()
fig.savefig("hero.png", dpi=120, bbox_inches="tight", facecolor=BG)
plt.show()








Figure 1: Multivariate signal with flagged anomalies. Red = detected; the tightened model stops flagging the normal correlated wobble.





The win was modeling the correlation between signals, so normal joint movement stopped tripping single-variable thresholds.

title: Cutting alert fatigue 35% for an ops monitoring team
text:
Decisions and tradeoffs
I moved from per-signal thresholding toward a multivariate approach that models the joint distribution, so a change is only anomalous relative to how the signals usually move together. Concretely, this meant PySpark modules that score correlation between payroll components rather than flagging each component against its own static threshold — the platform behind it was built config-driven and multi-algorithm on purpose, so it could plug into a new client’s front-end/back-end stack with minimal manual intervention rather than a rebuild per client.
